article_blocks.text: Strain Type: 80% Indica / 20% Sativa
Genetics: Mandarin × Purple #1
Breeder: Federation Seed Company
THC Content: 18–27%
CBD Content: Low
Terpene Profile: myrcene , limonene , caryophyllene
Primary Flavors: Raspberry, grapefruit, sweet citrus
Flowering Time (Indoor): 42–49 days
Outdoor Harvest Time: Early to late September
Indoor Yield: 400–500 g/m²
Outdoor Yield: High
Grow Difficulty: Easy to moderate

Mikado is an old Canadian marijuana strain whose reputation was built on traits that growers could immediately appreciate: remarkable speed, compact growth, heavy resin, large flowers, and a sweet fruit aroma that becomes much more expressive after curing. Federation Seed Company developed the strain during the early era of British Columbia seed breeding, and Mikado became one of the company’s recognizable indica offerings alongside cultivars such as Romulan and Island Sweet Skunk . Historical descriptions place its flowering cycle at only about 45 days, unusually fast even by modern standards, while mature flowers can display purple coloring, pink pistils, and a distinct wild-raspberry character. The strain also won the Nimbin Cup in 2000, helping cement its reputation among growers who valued old-school Canadian weed for performance rather than hype.
Genetics and Lineage

Mikado’s ancestry is unusually complicated because modern breeder information and historical cannabis records do not completely agree. The current Federation Seeds catalog describes the cultivar as an approximately 80/20 indica-dominant hybrid created from Mandarin × Purple #1. Older records, however, have long tied Mikado to Sweet Pink Grapefruit. Historical industry discussions went even further: breeder Steve of Spice of Life publicly stated that Mikado was essentially Federation’s version of the Sweet Pink Grapefruit material circulating in British Columbia during that era. Because of that conflict, it is more accurate to acknowledge both histories than to present one undocumented pedigree as indisputable fact.

Whatever the exact reconstruction of its family tree, the older Mikado phenotype was unmistakably indica in the garden. Federation’s period description characterized it as predominantly indica, fast maturing, heavily resinous, and capable of substantial production within approximately 45 days of flowering. The cultivar also became breeding material for Federation hybrids such as Big Mac, Crown Royal, Romulan × Mikado, and several later Mikado crosses, demonstrating that growers valued its rapid finish and compact structural traits enough to pass them into additional lines.

Its connection with Sweet Pink Grapefruit also makes considerable sensory sense. Classic Mikado descriptions repeatedly mention raspberry, grapefruit, sweet fruit, and citrus alongside deeper pine and Skunk notes. Whether modern Mandarin × Purple #1 seed stock should be regarded as an exact reproduction of the historical release is harder to establish. For collectors interested specifically in the old Federation version, provenance matters as much as the strain name.
Effects and Experience

Mikado’s experience is built around physical calm rather than explosive cerebral stimulation. The onset tends to begin with a warm body buzz that gradually reduces tension without immediately shutting down mental activity. Mood can become lighter, everyday irritations fade into the background, and sitting down with music, a movie, food, or relaxed conversation becomes increasingly appealing. Historical descriptions characterize the high as mellow, long-lasting, and particularly suited to evening use.

As the dose increases, the indica side becomes more obvious. Limbs can feel heavier, activity becomes less attractive, and appetite may become noticeably stronger. Modern commercial descriptions commonly portray Mikado as relaxing and somewhat sedating while still allowing reasonable functionality at moderate amounts. Current flower sold under the name has tested above 25% THC in some markets, illustrating how much stronger individual modern examples can be than generalized descriptions of the older cultivar might suggest.

There is no authoritative original THC specification from Federation’s early catalog material, so one fixed potency number would be misleading. Modern references range from roughly 18% into the mid-20s, but genetics, cultivation environment, harvest timing, and whether a crop actually descends from the old Federation stock all influence the result. Consumers should therefore judge the specific flower rather than assuming every Mikado sample delivers identical potency.
Medical Benefits

Mikado’s deeply calming physical character may appeal to medical cannabis consumers who prefer evening marijuana with less emphasis on mental stimulation. The gradual body relaxation may be useful for people seeking temporary relief from physical tension, stress, or difficulty settling down after the day. Its tendency to stimulate appetite may also be relevant for consumers who struggle to eat comfortably.

Historical and contemporary descriptions sometimes associate Mikado with pain, stress, anxiety, and sleep-related use, but these claims are based primarily on cannabis-consumer experience rather than clinical testing of the strain itself. Mikado has not been established through controlled trials as a treatment for chronic pain, insomnia, depression, anxiety disorders, or other medical conditions.

High-THC modern examples deserve particular caution. A cultivar traditionally described as mellow can still become overwhelming when flower tests in the mid-20% THC range. Medical marijuana consumers should review the cannabinoid profile of the actual batch whenever possible and adjust dosage according to personal tolerance.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Mikado’s fruit character separates it from the earthy Afghan-style indicas that dominated many early seed catalogs. Traditional descriptions emphasize wild raspberry, while later accounts frequently add grapefruit, citrus, and sweet berries. The growing plant can remain comparatively restrained aromatically, only for the cured flowers to develop a much fuller fruit-and-resin bouquet. The user’s existing KindGreenBuds Mikado archive also describes the classic expression as wild-raspberry flavored with purple leaves, squat flowers, and distinctly pink hairs at maturity.

Break apart a well-cured bud and sweet berry notes can give way to grapefruit peel, fresh vegetation, pine, and a deeper Skunk-like pungency. On inhalation, fruit tends to dominate first before a sweeter pine and earthy cannabis flavor develops through the finish. Modern strain descriptions similarly record fuel, grapefruit, citrus, berry, and pine characteristics.

No standardized terpene analysis survives from the original Federation release. Myrcene, limonene, caryophyllene, and pinene are plausible contributors to contemporary examples carrying berry, grapefruit, pine, and spice aromas, but those compounds should not be treated as a fixed chemical formula for an heirloom strain with several surviving versions.
Growing Information

Speed is Mikado’s defining cultivation advantage. Federation’s historical specification gives approximately 45 days of flowering, a mature height around five feet, and an outdoor harvest near the end of September. The plant develops long, jagged leaves and can produce visible resin not only on flowers but also along stems and foliage under strong lighting. Other historical descriptions place some outdoor plants even earlier, with harvest beginning in September or occasionally late August in favorable temperate environments.

Plant architecture is short, broad, and branch-oriented. Rather than stretching heavily after flowering begins, Mikado tends to spread outward and build thick flowering sites along sturdy branches. Historical accounts differ somewhat on the ideal indoor layout: original catalog material described it as suitable for Sea of Green, while later grow reports argued that allowing fewer plants to develop into larger multi-branched bushes produced better yields. In practice, both approaches can work depending on phenotype. Topping and moderate low-stress training suit the branchier expression particularly well.

Production is strong for such a quick-finishing indica. The current Federation listing estimates approximately 400–500 g/m² indoors and describes the strain as suitable for shorter northern seasons. Historical material listed individual plants around 10 ounces, while older outdoor descriptions reported the possibility of roughly a pound from well-developed specimens. Purple leaves and calyxes can emerge toward maturity, particularly under cooler temperatures, while pink pistils are one of the visual traits long associated with classic Mikado.
FAQ
Is Mikado an indica or sativa?
Mikado is predominantly indica. Historical Federation records describe it as an indica cultivar, while the current breeder listing places it around 80% indica and 20% sativa.
What are the genetics of Mikado?

The lineage is disputed. Federation Seeds currently lists Mandarin × Purple #1, while historical cannabis records strongly associate the original Federation Mikado with Sweet Pink Grapefruit genetics. For an authority reference, both histories should be acknowledged rather than hiding the discrepancy.
How long does Mikado take to flower?

The classic Federation strain is exceptionally fast, traditionally finishing in approximately 45 days after flowering begins. Modern Federation material broadens that slightly to around six to seven weeks.
What does Mikado taste like?

Classic Mikado combines raspberry, grapefruit, sweet citrus, pine, and earthy or Skunk-like notes. Some phenotypes become especially fruity after curing, while others develop a stronger resinous or fuel-like edge.
When is Mikado ready to harvest outdoors?

Historical Federation material places outdoor harvest around the end of September, although particularly early plants in favorable climates have been reported ready earlier in the month. Its short flowering cycle was one reason the cultivar became valuable in northern growing regions.
Final Thoughts on Mikado

Mikado represents a distinctly Canadian style of old-school cannabis breeding: fast enough for short seasons, compact enough for indoor rooms, resinous enough to satisfy experienced growers, and flavorful enough to remain memorable decades after its introduction. Its wild raspberry and grapefruit character, purple late-season coloring, pink pistils, and approximately six-week flowering cycle gave the strain a personality that went far beyond simple production efficiency.

The unresolved lineage is part of its history rather than something that should be concealed. Current Federation Seeds material identifies Mandarin × Purple #1, while older accounts connect the original cultivar closely with Sweet Pink Grapefruit. What remains consistent across those records is the plant itself—a predominantly indica weed with rapid maturation, heavy resin, substantial yields, fruity aromas, and a mellow long-lasting body high. For growers interested in classic British Columbia genetics, Mikado remains notable both as a practical cultivation strain and as an important survivor from Canada’s formative seed-breeding era.
